fields.Front: Why is requirements gathering critical in OODA?
fields.Back: It is the foundation of a successful project: translates user needs into functional and non-functional requirements and identifies key system objects, relationships, and behaviors.

fields.Front: What forms can requirements analysis take?
fields.Back: Natural language requirements; modelling requirements (UML visualizations, formulas, code); artifacts (goals, stakeholders, constraints).

fields.Front: What are functional requirements? Give two slide examples.
fields.Back: What the system should do: 'User can create a new account'; 'System should send an email after registration'.

fields.Text: Functional requirements map directly to {{c1::objects}} and their {{c2::behaviors (methods)}}.
'User can add books to the shopping cart' maps to objects `{{c1::Book}} and {{c2::ShoppingCart}} and method {{c3::addToCart()}}`.

fields.Front: What are non-functional requirements? Give two slide examples.
fields.Back: Define the quality of the system (performance, security, reliability): 'System must support 500 transactions per minute'; 'Response time should not exceed 2 seconds'.

fields.Front: How might 'System should handle 10,000 concurrent users' affect the design?
fields.Back: Infrastructure, class distribution, and architecture choices like multi-threading.

fields.Front: Requirements technique: interviews. What do you extract and how?
fields.Back: Nouns become potential objects; verbs become potential methods. 'The customer places an order' → Customer, Order, placeOrder().

fields.Front: Requirements technique: structured questionnaires. What is the example?
fields.Back: Gather input from many stakeholders to find common objects/methods; repeated 'login' requests → User and authenticate().

fields.Front: Requirements technique: observation. What is the example?
fields.Back: Watching users of existing systems reveals implicit requirements; users placing items in a physical cart → ShoppingCart and addItem().

fields.Text: {{c1::Functional}} requirements say what the system should do; {{c2::non-functional}} requirements define the quality of the system.
In interviews, {{c1::nouns}} suggest potential objects and {{c2::verbs}} suggest potential methods.
Three requirements-gathering techniques from the slides: {{c1::interviews}}, {{c2::structured questionnaires}}, and {{c3::observation}}.
